mainTopic: How damage is valued when an ox's worth changes, and how רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה read 'divide the live ox and the dead'
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about a creditor who grabs an ox that did damage. The גמרא rejects the idea that a later creditor who collects first loses what he took. The ox case is special, because the injured party collects from that very ox wherever it is. Next, a ברייתא teaches when damage is valued. If the hurt ox later rises in value, we go by the time of the damage. If it drops because of the wound, we go by the time of court. The גמרא explains the ruling about the damaging ox according to רבי עקיבא, who holds that the two owners are partners, by saying its owner fattened it. Then a new משנה brings the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה about which case the פסוק 'sell the live ox and divide its money, and the dead too they shall divide' describes. רבא shows that they really differ about who carries a drop in the carcass's value. אביי begins to challenge him, and that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Trying to learn a rule about a later creditor who collects first
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא voids the creditor's grab even when the damage came before the loan. The גמרא tries to learn from this that a later creditor's collection is not valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even if the ox did damage before the owner owed money, the creditor got there first and grabbed it! Should we learn from this that a later creditor who collects first does not get to keep what he took?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points to the case where the damage came first and the creditor's loan came later, yet the creditor grabbed the ox first. It tries to learn a general rule from this case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this case the injured party's claim is older, but the creditor actually took the ox first. The ברייתא still says the creditor's grab does not work. So the גמרא suggests a broad rule: a בעל חוב מאוחר who collects before the earlier claimant loses what he collected.

keyTerms.meaning: A creditor, someone who is owed money
Came first, got there earlier
Learn from this, conclude from it
Later, the one whose claim came second
Collected payment

phrases.english: And even if it did damage before he owed money,
the creditor came first!
Learn from this,
that a later creditor who went ahead and collected,
what he collected is not really collected?!

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, בַּעַל חוֹב מְאוּחָר שֶׁקָּדַם וְגָבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the discussion of the ברייתא about a creditor seizing a damaging ox, which began on the earlier part of the daf.
steps.raayaObject: A later creditor who collects ahead of an earlier claimant does not keep what he collected.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's ruling that a creditor's seizure of the ox does nothing, even when the damage came before the loan.

steps.title: Rejecting the inference: the ox case is special
steps.stepSummary: No, a later creditor's collection normally stands. The ox case is different because the injured party is paid from the very ox that hurt him, no matter who holds it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, really I can tell you that what he collected stays collected. But there it is different, because the injured party can say to the creditor: 'If the ox were sitting with you, wouldn't I collect it from you? This ox that damaged me is the one I get paid from.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the big rule from Step 1. It explains that the ox case has its own special reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The injured party's right is tied to the damaging ox itself, not just to the owner's money in general. So wherever the ox goes, even into the creditor's hands, the injured party can take it from there. That is why the creditor's grab fails, and it tells us nothing about creditors in general.

keyTerms.meaning: Really, actually (the original idea still stands)
There it is different
Ox
I get paid

steps.whatToRemember: Normally a later creditor who collects first keeps what he took. The damaging ox is an exception, because the injured party collects from that very ox wherever it is.
steps.confusionAlert: This step does not say that creditors lose out in general. The ox is an exception with its own special reason.
steps.whyThisMatters: It keeps the general rule מה שגבה גבה in place. It also shows that the injured party's claim is attached to the damaging animal itself.

phrases.english: No, really I can tell you:
what he collected stays collected;
but there it is different,
because he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The injured party is speaking to the creditor who grabbed the ox.

phrases.english: If it were with you,
wouldn't I collect it from you?
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The meaning is the same either way.

phrases.english: For this ox that damaged me,
from it I get paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, לְעוֹלָם אֵימָא לָךְ: מַה שֶּׁגָּבָה גָּבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference drawn in Step 1.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the general rule that a later creditor's collection is void; it only limits the ruling to the damaging-ox case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof ignored that the injured party's claim is tied to the specific ox, which he can take from anyone who holds it.

steps.title: A ברייתא: if the hurt ox gains value, we use the value at the time of damage
steps.stepSummary: An ox lost fifty זוז of value when it was gored. It later rose in value, and would have been worth even more without the injury. The payment is based on the time of the damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: An ox worth two hundred gored another ox worth two hundred and injured it by fifty זוז. The hurt ox then rose in value and was worth four hundred זוז, while without the injury it would have been worth eight hundred זוז. The payment follows the time of the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a ברייתא about when to measure the damage. Here the hurt ox later goes up in value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The loss today looks huge: four hundred versus eight hundred. But the damage is measured as it was when it happened, which is fifty זוז, and the goring ox's owner pays based on that. Any later growth in value does not make his payment bigger.

keyTerms.meaning: Gored
Injured, wounded
Rose in value
According to the time of the damage

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
An ox worth two hundred
that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and injured it by fifty zuz,

phrases.aramaic: וְשָׁבַח וְעָמַד עַל אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת זוּז –
phrases.english: and it rose in value and stood at four hundred zuz,
while if it had not injured it,

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה עוֹמֵד עַל שְׁמֹנֶה מֵאוֹת זוּז;
phrases.english: it would have stood at eight hundred zuz;
he pays according to the time of the damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a new topic: at what time the damage is valued.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the injured ox later rises in value, payment is based on the damage at the time it happened.

steps.title: If the hurt ox loses value, we use the value at the time of the court case
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא continues. If the injured ox later drops in value, the damage is measured at the time it stands in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it lost value, the damage is measured by its value at the time it stands in court.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes with the opposite case, where the hurt ox later loses value. This time the court date sets the measure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the ox drops in value, the later and lower value is used, so the owner of the goring ox pays more. Put simply, a rise in value after the injury does not raise the payment, but a drop in value after the injury does.

keyTerms.meaning: Lost value, became weaker
Standing in court, the time of the court case

steps.whatToRemember: If the hurt ox gains value later, we use the value at the time of the damage. If it loses value later, we use the value at the time of the court case.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. A rise in value uses the time of the damage, and a drop in value uses the time of court.

phrases.english: If it lost value,
phrases.notes: This is still about the hurt ox, which became weaker or cheaper after the injury.

phrases.english: according to the time of standing in court.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּחַשׁ – כִּשְׁעַת הַעֲמָדָה בַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא from Step 3 with the opposite case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the injured ox later drops in value, the damage is measured at the time of the court case.

steps.title: The damaging ox goes up or down in value
steps.stepSummary: If the מזיק ox went up in value, payment follows the time of the damage. If it went down, payment follows the time of court.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the ox that did the damage went up in value, its owner pays based on the time of the damage. If it went down in value, he pays based on the time they stand in court.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going. It now gives two rules about the ox that did the damage instead of the ox that was hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Payment here comes from the body of the damaging ox, so its value matters. A rise in value does not help the injured party; he gets only what the ox was worth when it did the damage. A drop in value does hurt him; he gets only what the ox is worth at the time of court.

keyTerms.meaning: The one that did the damage; here, the ox that gored
Went up in value
Went down in value, got thinner
The time the damage happened
The time the case stands in court

steps.confusionAlert: Steps 3-4 were about the injured ox (the ניזק). Here the ברייתא switches to the ox that did the damage (the מזיק). Keep track of which ox is changing in value.

phrases.english: If the ox that did the damage went up in value,
phrases.notes: Now we are talking about the goring ox, not the ox that was hurt.

phrases.english: he pays him based on the time of the damage.
If it went down in value, he pays based on the time of standing in court.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁבַח מַזִּיק – נוֹתֵן לוֹ כִּשְׁעַת הַנֶּזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, moving from the injured ox to the damaging ox.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A rise in the מזיק ox's value: pay by the time of damage. A drop: pay by the time of court.

steps.title: Whose opinion is the first ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose view the first ruling follows. It suggests רבי ישמעאל, who holds the injured party is just a בעל חוב owed money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: if the damaging ox went up in value, he pays based on the time of the damage. Whose view is this? It is רבי ישמעאל, who says the injured party is a creditor, and he is only owed money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the first ruling and asks which תנא it fits. It answers that it seems to be רבי ישמעאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the injured party is only a בעל חוב, he is owed a fixed amount of money and owns no part of the ox. So when the ox goes up in value, the extra value is not his. That fits a payment based on the time of the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this?
A creditor, someone who is owed money
Money (literally, zuz coins)

phrases.english: The Master said: If the ox that did the damage went up in value,
he pays based on the time of the damage.
Whose view is this? It is רבי ישמעאל,
who says: he is a creditor,
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner of the injured ox. He is owed a debt; he does not own a share of the ox.

phrases.english: and it is money that he is owed by him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: שָׁבַח מַזִּיק – נוֹתֵן כִּשְׁעַת הַנֶּזֶק. מַנִּי – רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which תנא the first rule of step 5 follows.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא is behind the rule that a rise in the מזיק's value is judged by the time of damage?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי ישמעאל, who holds the injured party is a בעל חוב owed money.

steps.title: The second ruling fits רבי עקיבא, so the ברייתא is split
steps.stepSummary: The second ruling, paying by the time of court when the ox loses value, fits רבי עקיבא, who holds they are partners. Would one ברייתא switch opinions halfway?
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end: if it went down in value, he pays based on the time of court. Now we have reached רבי עקיבא, who says they are partners! Could the first part be רבי ישמעאל and the end be רבי עקיבא?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the suggestion from step 6. The second ruling seems to follow the opposite view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Partners share both gains and losses. When the ox loses value, the injured party loses with it, and that fits רבי עקיבא's partnership view. But then the first ruling, where he does not share in the gain, would follow רבי ישמעאל, and one ברייתא would be split between two opposing views.

keyTerms.meaning: "Say the end": look at the next clause
"We have reached" a certain opinion
Partners, co-owners of the ox
The first part of the teaching

phrases.english: Say the end of the teaching:
If it went down in value, he pays based on the time of standing in court.
Now we have reached רבי עקיבא,
who says: they are partners!
phrases.notes: The two owners share the goring ox, so the injured side shares in its loss.

phrases.english: The first part is רבי ישמעאל
and the end is רבי עקיבא?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֵימָא סֵיפָא: כָּחַשׁ – כִּשְׁעַת הַעֲמָדָה בַּדִּין. אֲתָאן לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the attribution to רבי ישמעאל in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא follows רבי ישמעאל.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second ruling (sharing the loss) fits only the partnership view of רבי עקיבא, so the ברייתא would be split between two opposing תנאים.

steps.title: It is all רבי עקיבא: the owner fattened the ox
steps.stepSummary: The whole ברייתא follows רבי עקיבא. The first ruling speaks of an ox that went up in value because its owner fattened it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is all רבי עקיבא. What case are we dealing with here? Where the owner fattened the ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It puts the whole ברייתא under רבי עקיבא by explaining the first case in a specific way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even partners do not share in a gain that one of them produced with his own work and expense. The ox went up in value only because its owner fattened it, so that extra value belongs to him alone. That is why the injured partner is still paid based on the time of the damage.

keyTerms.meaning: All of it, the whole teaching
"What case are we dealing with here?": the גמרא narrows the case
He fattened it

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא follows רבי עקיבא's partnership view. The injured party shares in natural losses of the damaging ox, but not in a rise in value that came from the owner fattening it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that partnership in the ox does not cover value the owner added through his own effort.

phrases.english: No, it is all רבי עקיבא;
and what case are we dealing with here?
phrases.notes: "Here" means the first ruling, where the damaging ox went up in value.

phrases.english: Where he fattened it.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, כּוּלַּהּ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא הִיא; וְהָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – כְּשֶׁפִּיטְּמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 7 by narrowing the case of the first ruling.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) so that both rulings fit one תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first ruling seemed to follow רבי ישמעאל, because the injured party did not share in the gain.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both rulings follow רבי עקיבא. The gain was from the owner fattening the ox, and a partner does not share in that.

steps.title: If it means fattened, the first clause is too obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from Step 8. If 'went up in value' means 'fattened', then the רישא, where the hurt ox went up and the payment is by the time of the damage, would be too obvious to say.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the ברייתא is talking about an ox its owner fattened, look at the first clause: the hurt ox went up in value to 400 זוז, and the one who caused the damage pays by the time of the damage. If that means the owner fattened it, why would we need to be told that?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the answer from Step 8. It shows that the 'fattened' explanation would make the first clause of the ברייתא pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Pays by the time of the damage' means the one who caused the damage pays only for the 50 זוז loss, not for the bigger 400-זוז gap that shows up later. If the owner of the hurt ox fattened it himself, it is obvious that the one who caused the damage should not have to pay for value the owner was adding with his own feeding. A ברייתא does not waste words on something that obvious, so the 'fattened' reading seems to cause a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: He fattened it (fed it so it gained weight and value)
The first clause of a ברייתא or משנה
It went up in value
Does this need to be said? (it is obvious)

phrases.english: If it is where he fattened it,
say the first clause:

phrases.aramaic: שָׁבַח וְעָמַד עַל אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת זוּז –
phrases.english: it went up in value and stood at four hundred zuz –
phrases.notes: This clause is about the hurt ox, the one that got gored.

phrases.english: he pays him according to the time of the damage.
If it is where he fattened it, does it need to be said?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי כְּשֶׁפִּיטְּמוֹ, אֵימָא רֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the 'fattened' explanation given in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that the ברייתא is talking about a fattened ox.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the רישא is also about a fattened ox, its ruling is obvious, so it would not need to be taught.

steps.title: The first clause covers both cases, the last clause only fattening
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the רישא is true whether the ox was fattened or rose in value by itself. It is needed to teach the case where it rose by itself. Only the סיפא has to be about a fattened ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: you can find the first clause true either way, whether the owner fattened the ox or it went up in value by itself. It was needed to teach us that even when it went up by itself, the one who caused the damage pays by the time of the damage. The last clause, though, can only be a case where the owner fattened it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends the 'fattened' answer. He says the two clauses do not have to describe the same kind of rise in value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא is not limited to fattening. Its new lesson is the case where the hurt ox went up by itself. You might think the injured owner could say, 'Without your goring it would be worth 800,' and claim the bigger gap. The ברייתא teaches that even then, the one who caused the damage pays only by the time of the damage. The סיפא is about the ox that did the damage, and under רבי עקיבא it has to mean fattening. So the answer from Step 8 stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: You can find it (the ruling applies in this case)
By itself, without anyone doing anything
It was needed to teach us
The last clause

steps.whatToRemember: The רישא (hurt ox went up in value) covers both fattening and natural growth, and it teaches the natural-growth case. The סיפא (ox that did the damage went up in value) is only about fattening, so it fits רבי עקיבא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two oxen. The רישא is about the ox that got hurt. The סיפא is about the ox that did the damage. The 'fattened' answer is only needed for the סיפא.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: The first clause –
you can find it whether he actually fattened it
or whether it went up in value by itself,
and it was needed to teach us
that where it went up in value by itself –
he pays him according to the time of the damage.
The last clause – you cannot find it
except where he fattened it.
phrases.notes: This is the clause about the ox that did the damage going up in value, from Step 5.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: רֵישָׁא – מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Separates the two clauses: the רישא is broad, and the סיפא is narrow.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both clauses had to be about fattening, which would make the רישא obvious.
steps.terutzMaskana: The רישא covers natural growth too, and that is its lesson. Only the סיפא needs fattening.

steps.title: Why did the hurt ox get weaker?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling that a hurt ox that got weaker is measured at the time of court, and asks what made it weaker.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא said: if the hurt ox got weaker, it is measured by its value at the time it stands in court. What made it weaker?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next clause of the ברייתא (from Step 4) and asks a question about the case. This sets up the next two steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measuring at the time of court means the one who caused the damage pays more, because the ox is now worth even less. That is only fair if the drop in value is really his fault. So the גמרא needs to know what caused it.

keyTerms.meaning: It got weaker or lost value
The time it stands in court
Because of what?

phrases.english: If it got weaker – it is measured by the time of standing in court.
phrases.notes: This quotes the ruling about the hurt ox from Step 4.

phrases.english: It got weaker because of what?

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּחַשׁ מֵחֲמַת מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a different clause of the same ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What caused the hurt ox to lose value after the injury.

steps.title: It cannot mean it got weaker from work
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the ox got weaker from work, and rejects that idea. The one who caused the damage could say: 'You weakened it, so why should I pay?'
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it got weaker because it was worked hard, he could answer him: 'You made it weaker, and I should pay?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries one possible answer to its question and shows right away that it does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner of the hurt ox worked it and that made it weaker, the loss is his own doing. It would not be fair to make the one who caused the damage pay for it, so the ruling cannot be talking about that case.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that is about to be rejected)
Work, labor

phrases.english: If you say it got weaker because of work,
let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The one who caused the damage is speaking to the owner of the hurt ox.

phrases.english: You made it weaker, and I should pay?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵימָא דְּכָחֲשָׁה מֵחֲמַת מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries an answer to the question in Step 11 and rejects it.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the suggestion that the ox got weaker from work.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The loss would come from the owner's own actions, so it is unfair to charge the one who caused the damage.

steps.title: It got weaker from the wound itself
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the ox got weaker from the wound. The injured owner can say: 'Your ox's horn is still buried in it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: it is a case where the ox got weaker because of the wound. The injured owner can tell him: 'The horn of your ox is buried in it.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives the real answer to the question in Step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the loss comes from the wound itself, it is still part of the damage the goring ox did. That is why the payment waits until court, so the full drop in value is counted.

keyTerms.meaning: The wound or injury
Your ox's horn
Buried (still stuck inside)

steps.whatToRemember: A hurt ox that loses value is measured at the time of court only when the loss comes from the wound itself. A loss caused by its owner working it does not count.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It is where it got weaker because of the wound,
for he can say to him:
phrases.notes: Now the owner of the hurt ox is the one speaking.

phrases.english: The horn of your ox is buried in it.
phrases.notes: This is a picture: the goring is still doing damage, as if the horn were still stuck inside.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: דִּכְחַשׁ מֵחֲמַת מַכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 11 after the rejection in Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ox lost value because of the wound, and that loss is the fault of the one who caused the damage.

steps.title: New משנה: רבי מאיר applies the פסוק to an ox whose carcass is worthless
steps.stepSummary: An ox worth 200 kills an ox worth 200 and the carcass is worth nothing. רבי מאיר says this is the case the פסוק means by 'sell the live ox and divide its money.'
steps.simpleTranslation: An ox worth two hundred gored and killed another ox worth two hundred, and the dead body is worth nothing. רבי מאיר said: this is the case the פסוק describes, 'Then they shall sell the live ox and divide its money.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. רבי מאיר names the exact case the פסוק about splitting the live ox is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both oxen are worth 200, and the dead ox is now worth nothing. If you sell the live ox and split the money, each owner gets 100. That means the owner of the dead ox gets half of his 200 loss, which is the half-damage payment.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה being studied
Gored
The carcass, the dead animal's body
Worth anything (here: 'worth nothing')
And they shall divide its money

phrases.english: MISHNAH: An ox worth two hundred
that gored an ox worth two hundred,
phrases.notes: 'Gored' here means it killed the other ox. That is why the next words talk about the carcass.

phrases.english: and the carcass is worth nothing –

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר, עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir said: about this it is stated:
"Then they shall sell the live ox
and divide its money."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר, עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה. It is not connected to the ברייתא about changes in the oxen's value discussed in Steps 3-13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, the פסוק 'sell the live ox and divide its money' describes two oxen worth 200 each, where the carcass is worthless.

steps.title: רבי יהודה agrees with the money result but says the reading skips part of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה agrees with the payment. But he objects that רבי מאיר's case leaves no room for the words 'and the dead too they shall divide.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said to him: That is indeed the law. But you have explained 'sell the live ox and divide its money,' and you have not explained 'and the dead too they shall divide'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה pushes back on רבי מאיר. He does not disagree about who pays what. He disagrees about how to read the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the carcass is worth nothing, there is nothing to divide from the dead ox. So the second half of the פסוק, 'the dead too they shall divide,' has no meaning in רבי מאיר's case. רבי יהודה says the case the פסוק describes must be one where the carcass has some value.

keyTerms.meaning: And so is the law (I agree with the ruling)
You have fulfilled, meaning you have given meaning to this part of the פסוק
And the dead too they shall divide

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה is NOT saying רבי מאיר's ruling is wrong. 'וכן הלכה' means he agrees about the money. His objection is only that רבי מאיר's case does not fit every word of the פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: וְכֵן הֲלָכָה;
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said to him: And so is the law;
you have fulfilled "Then they shall sell the live ox
and divide its money,"
but you have not fulfilled "And the dead too they shall divide"!
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק, שמות 21:35.

steps.triggerLanguage: קִיַּימְתָּ ״וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ״, וְלֹא קִיַּימְתָּ ״וְגַם הַמֵּת יֶחֱצוּן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי מאיר's reading of the פסוק in Step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's claim that the פסוק describes a case where the carcass is worthless
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A worthless carcass leaves nothing to divide, so the words 'and the dead too they shall divide' would have no meaning in that case.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's own case: the carcass is worth fifty זוז
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says the פסוק describes an ox worth 200 that killed an ox worth 200 whose carcass is worth 50. Each owner takes half the live ox and half the dead ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then which case is it? An ox worth two hundred gored an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth fifty זוז. This owner takes half the live ox and half the dead one, and that owner takes half the live ox and half the dead one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה asks his own question, 'which case is it?', and answers it. He gives a case that fits both halves of the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the carcass is worth 50, there really is something to divide from the dead ox too. Each owner gets 100 from the live ox and 25 from the carcass, so each ends up with 125. The loss from the death was 150, and each side carries half of it (75).

keyTerms.meaning: And which one? (Which case does the פסוק mean?)
A coin, the same as a דינר
Takes
Half the live ox and half the dead ox

phrases.english: And which case is it? It is an ox worth two hundred
that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth fifty zuz;

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁזֶּה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: so that this one takes half the live ox and half the dead one,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת.
phrases.english: and that one takes half the live ox and half the dead one.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵיזֶה? זֶה שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After objecting in Step 15, רבי יהודה offers his own case that fits the whole פסוק.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case does the פסוק describe, if it is not רבי מאיר's case?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two oxen worth 200 each, where the carcass is worth 50. Both owners split the live ox and the carcass equally.
steps.whatToRemember: In the משנה, both תנאים agree on the basic payment (וכן הלכה). They argue about which case the פסוק is describing. רבי מאיר says a worthless carcass. רבי יהודה says a carcass worth 50, so that 'the dead too they shall divide' has meaning. Step 22 shows that their views still differ in one practical case.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives רבי יהודה's view in full
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא with רבי יהודה's case of a carcass worth 50 and says outright that this is 'the ox stated in the תורה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: An ox worth two hundred gored an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth fifty זוז. This owner takes half the live ox and half the dead one, and that owner takes half the live ox and half the dead one. This is the ox the תורה speaks about. These are the words of רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens by bringing a ברייתא. It repeats רבי יהודה's view and labels it clearly as his.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds the clear statement 'this is the ox stated in the תורה.' That makes the argument plain: it is about which case the פסוק describes. It also prepares for רבי מאיר's fuller answer in the next lines.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה
That is stated in the תורה

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שָׁוֶה מָאתַיִם,
phrases.english: An ox worth two hundred that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth fifty zuz –

phrases.aramaic: זֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: this one takes half the live ox and half the dead one,

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה נוֹטֵל חֲצִי הַחַי וַחֲצִי הַמֵּת,
phrases.english: and that one takes half the live ox and half the dead one,
and this is the ox stated in the Torah;
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא begins by bringing a ברייתא that restates רבי יהודה's view from Step 16 more fully.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, the ox in the פסוק is the case of a carcass worth 50, where both sides split the live ox and the carcass.

steps.title: In the ברייתא, רבי מאיר says the תורה's case is the worthless carcass
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר rejects רבי יהודה's case as the case in the תורה. He says the פסוק describes a carcass worth nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: That is not the ox the תורה speaks about. Rather, it is an ox worth two hundred that gored an ox worth two hundred, and the carcass is worth nothing. About this the פסוק says: 'Then they shall sell the live ox and divide its money.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with רבי מאיר's side. He directly denies that the 50-זוז case is what the תורה means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבי מאיר openly says 'this is not the ox stated in the תורה.' He keeps his case of a worthless carcass. This sets up the question in the next step: how does he explain 'the dead too they shall divide'?

keyTerms.meaning: This is not
Rather
It is stated (in the פסוק)

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
This is not the ox stated in the Torah,
rather, an ox worth two hundred
that gored an ox worth two hundred,
and the carcass is worth nothing,
about this it is stated:

phrases.aramaic: ״וּמָכְרוּ אֶת הַשּׁוֹר הַחַי וְחָצוּ אֶת כַּסְפּוֹ״.
phrases.english: "Then they shall sell the live ox and divide its money."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אֵין זֶהוּ שׁוֹר הָאָמוּר בַּתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to רבי יהודה's statement in Step 17, inside the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, the ox in the פסוק is the case of a worthless carcass.

steps.title: רבי מאיר asks himself how he explains 'the dead too they shall divide'
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר raises רבי יהודה's objection on his own: if the carcass is worthless, what do the words 'and the dead too they shall divide' mean?
steps.simpleTranslation: But how do I explain 'And the dead too they shall divide'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר asks the question that רבי יהודה raised in the משנה. This line sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same problem from Step 15. In the ברייתא, רבי מאיר takes it on himself and promises to give those words a meaning that fits his case.

keyTerms.meaning: How do I fulfill, meaning how do I explain these words

phrases.english: But how do I fulfill
"And the dead too they shall divide"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מָה אֲנִי מְקַיֵּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After stating his reading in Step 18, רבי מאיר raises the obvious problem with it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What do the words 'and the dead too they shall divide' mean if the carcass in the פסוק's case is worth nothing?

steps.title: רבי מאיר: the loss caused by the death is split and paid from the live ox
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר explains that 'divide the dead' means dividing the loss the death caused, and that loss is paid out of the live ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: The loss that death caused the ox is divided, and it is paid from the live ox.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר answers his own question. 'Dividing the dead' does not mean splitting the carcass. It means splitting the loss caused by the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, the words 'the dead too they shall divide' teach that both sides share the drop in value caused by the death, and the payment comes from the live ox. The carcass itself is not split between them. This is the difference from רבי יהודה, who has both sides take half of the carcass.

keyTerms.meaning: The loss in value
That death caused it to lose
They divide it from the live ox

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה: 'divide the dead' means splitting the carcass itself. רבי מאיר: it means splitting the loss caused by the death, paid from the live ox.

phrases.english: The loss that death caused it –
they divide it from the live ox.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּחָת שֶׁפְּחָתַתּוּ מִיתָה מַחֲצִין בַּחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'The dead too they shall divide' refers to splitting the loss caused by the death, paid out of the live ox, and not to splitting the carcass.

steps.title: If both opinions give each side 125, what is the difference?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that in the case of a carcass worth 50, both רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה give each owner 125. So it asks what the practical difference between them is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look: whether you follow רבי מאיר or רבי יהודה, this owner takes 125 and that owner takes 125. So what is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sees that the two opinions give the same money result in this case. It asks what the two תנאים are actually arguing about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי מאיר, the injured owner keeps the carcass (50) and gets half of the 150 loss (75) from the live ox, which totals 125. Under רבי יהודה, each owner takes half of 200 plus half of 50, which is also 125. Since the numbers match, the גמרא wants to find a case where the two methods would give different results.

keyTerms.meaning: Now look, since it is so (opens a point both sides agree on)
takes, receives
What is the difference between them?

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה is pointless. The final split is the same here, but their reasons are different, and the next step shows a case where that difference matters.

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי בֵּין רַבִּי מֵאִיר בֵּין רַבִּי יְהוּדָה –
phrases.english: Now look, whether according to Rabbi Meir or according to Rabbi Yehuda,
this one takes one hundred and twenty-five,
phrases.notes: Under רבי מאיר it is the carcass (50) plus half the 150 loss (75). Under רבי יהודה it is half of 200 plus half of 50.

phrases.english: and that one takes one hundred and twenty-five;
what is the difference between them?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדֵי בֵּין רַבִּי מֵאִיר בֵּין רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the outcome of רבי יהודה's method (step 16) with רבי מאיר's method (step 20) and finds they give the same result.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה would give different results.

steps.title: They disagree about who absorbs a drop in the carcass's value
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the difference is when the carcass loses value before it is sold. According to רבי מאיר, the injured owner absorbs that loss. According to רבי יהודה, the damager absorbs half of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The difference between them is the drop in the carcass's value. רבי מאיר holds that the drop belongs to the injured owner. רבי יהודה holds that half of the drop belongs to the one who caused the damage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question by naming a case where the two opinions give different results: the carcass gets cheaper after the death.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי מאיר, the carcass belongs completely to the injured owner, and the damager only pays half of the loss the death caused. So if the carcass later loses value, that is the injured owner's own problem. For רבי יהודה, both owners share the dead ox, so if it loses value, each one loses half.

keyTerms.meaning: the drop in the carcass's value
the injured party, the one whose property was damaged
the damager, the owner of the ox that did the damage
half
holds, is of the opinion

steps.whatToRemember: Same split on paper (125 each), but different ownership. For רבי מאיר, the carcass belongs only to the ניזק. For רבי יהודה, both owners share it. So any later drop in the carcass's value shows the difference.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the two readings of the פסוק lead to a real difference in practice, not just a difference in how the case is described.

phrases.english: Rava said:
The drop in the carcass's value is the difference between them.
phrases.notes: He means the carcass gets cheaper between the time the ox dies and the time it is sold.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir holds:
the drop in the carcass's value is the injured party's loss,
and Rabbi Yehuda holds:
half of the drop in the carcass's value is the damager's loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: פְּחַת נְבֵילָה אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21 by identifying the practical difference.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two opinions differ when the carcass drops in value. Under רבי מאיר the ניזק absorbs all of it. Under רבי יהודה the מזיק absorbs half.

steps.title: אביי begins to challenge רבא's explanation of רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: אביי starts to object to רבא: if רבי יהודה really makes the damager share the carcass's drop in value, that leads to a problem. His challenge continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If so, we find that according to רבי יהודה...
steps.whatsHappening: אביי is setting up a challenge against רבא's answer. The sentence is not finished here and continues in the next part of the גמרא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'if so' show that אביי is taking רבא's explanation of רבי יהודה (the damager shares the carcass's loss) and is about to show a strange result that comes from it. The actual problem is stated on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: if so, if that is true
we find, it turns out

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
If so, we find according to Rabbi Yehuda

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: אִם כֵּן, מָצִינוּ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts an objection to רבא's answer in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that according to רבי יהודה the מזיק absorbs half of the carcass's drop in value.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'If so' introduces an unacceptable result that follows from רבא's explanation. The full result is stated in the next section.
